🎓 Exam pearl. The magic phrase is "arterial hyperenhancement with washout" in a cirrhotic liver = HCC, no biopsy needed. Haemangioma fills in centripetally and follows blood pool; FNH has a central scar enhancing late; metastases are hypodense on portal venous. Match the pattern to the phase and the diagnosis writes itself.
The pancreatic-protocol CT is a dedicated dual-phase study using a pancreatic (late arterial, ~40s) phase and a portal venous (~70s) phase to maximise contrast between the normally-enhancing gland and pathology. Its two big finals-level jobs are staging pancreatic adenocarcinoma (resectability) and assessing the severity and complications of acute pancreatitis.
1Get the phases right
A single portal-venous scan can miss a small tumour. The pancreatic phase (~40s) shows the pancreas enhancing brightly, so a hypoenhancing (hypodense) adenocarcinoma stands out and arterial anatomy (SMA, coeliac axis) is opacified. The portal venous phase (~70s) best demonstrates liver metastases, nodal disease and the SMV/portal vein.
Pancreatic ~40sPortal venous ~70s
2Pancreatic cancer: the mass and the ducts
Adenocarcinoma is usually a hypoenhancing mass in the head, often presenting with painless obstructive jaundice and weight loss. It classically obstructs both ducts, producing the double duct sign — simultaneous dilatation of the common bile duct and the pancreatic duct.
Painless jaundice + head mass→Double duct sign = pancreatic Ca
3Assess resectability by vessels
CT decides operability by looking at vascular involvement. Assess the SMA, coeliac axis and SMV/portal vein: tumour contact >180° (encasement) usually means locally advanced / unresectable, whereas abutment <180° may be borderline. Also hunt for liver and peritoneal metastases and distant nodes. Only a minority are resectable — head lesions may proceed to a Whipple's (pancreaticoduodenectomy).
🩸Encasement >180°
SMA/coeliac/SMV involvement → usually unresectable.
🔪Resectable head lesion
No vessel encasement, no mets → Whipple's candidate.
4Acute pancreatitis: when and what
Diagnosis is clinical + amylase/lipase — CT is not needed early for diagnosis. Scan at ~72h+ to grade severity and complications: pancreatic necrosis (non-enhancing gland), peripancreatic collections (acute fluid collections, pseudocyst, walled-off necrosis), infected necrosis, haemorrhage and vascular complications (splenic vein thrombosis, pseudoaneurysm). Causes follow GET SMASHED (gallstones and alcohol commonest); severity scored with Glasgow/APACHE II plus the CT severity index.
  • CT too early = normal-looking pancreas → falsely reassuring.
  • Non-enhancing parenchyma on the venous phase = necrosis.
🚩
Severe acute pancreatitis with organ failure, extensive or infected necrosis (gas within a collection) or haemorrhage is life-threatening — needs HDU/ITU, specialist input and possible intervention. Conversely, painless obstructive jaundice + weight loss + a pancreatic head mass (double duct) is pancreatic cancer until proven otherwise and needs urgent HPB MDT referral.

🎓 Exam pearl. Two triggers to memorise: painless obstructive jaundice with a hypodense head mass + double duct sign = pancreatic cancer (assess vessel encasement >180° for resectability, then HPB MDT); and in acute pancreatitis don't CT early — scan at ~72h+ for necrosis/collections, and gas in a collection = infected necrosis needing urgent intervention.
A CT urogram (CTU) is a multiphase contrast-enhanced CT of the urinary tract, acquired across a non-contrast, nephrographic and delayed excretory phase. In the excretory phase, contrast excreted by the kidneys opacifies the collecting system, ureters and bladder, so the entire upper tract can be surveyed in a single study. It is the investigation of choice for visible (frank) haematuria, hunting for renal cell and upper-tract urothelial tumours.
1Why and when — the haematuria pathway
Visible haematuria is a red-flag symptom triggering an urgent 2-week-wait (2WW) referral for suspected urological cancer. NICE criteria: visible haematuria in adults ≥45, or ≥60 with unexplained non-visible haematuria plus dysuria or a raised WCC. The standard work-up pairs two tests that cover different territory.
CT urogram — upper tractFlexible cystoscopy — bladder
Bladder cancer is the commonest cause of visible haematuria — cystoscopy is essential and is NOT replaced by CTU.
2The phases — what each one shows
A multiphase protocol gives complementary information across the study.
  • Non-contrast — detects calculi (all stones are dense here, even radiolucent uric-acid stones) and baseline calcification.
  • Nephrographic — parenchymal enhancement; an enhancing solid renal mass is renal cell carcinoma (RCC) until proven otherwise.
  • Delayed excretory — contrast opacifies the collecting system and ureters; look for filling defects and strictures.
3Key findings — filling defects and masses
On the excretory phase, a filling defect within the contrast column of the collecting system or ureter suggests an upper-tract urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma — though a non-opaque stone or clot can mimic it. Correlate with the non-contrast phase to exclude a stone.
Filling defect in opacified ureter→Urothelial (TCC) tumour until excluded
Enhancing solid renal mass→RCC until proven otherwise
🩻Renal cell carcinoma
Enhancing solid mass on nephrographic phase; commonest renal malignancy.
🩻Urothelial (TCC)
Filling defect / stricture in collecting system; smoking & aromatic amines are risk factors.
🪨Calculi / obstruction
Dense on non-contrast phase; excretory phase shows hydronephrosis / delayed excretion.
4Strengths and trade-offs
A single CTU images the whole urinary tract — kidneys, collecting systems, ureters and bladder — and also characterises complex stones and congenital anomalies. The cost is a significant iodinated contrast load (caution in renal impairment) and a higher radiation dose than single-phase CT.
🚩
Visible haematuria is urological cancer until proven otherwise. Do not attribute frank haematuria to a UTI in an at-risk adult without excluding malignancy. Refer urgently on a 2-week-wait pathway for CT urogram AND flexible cystoscopy. An enhancing renal mass is RCC until proven otherwise.

📷 Image placeholder — Nephrographic-phase axial CT: a heterogeneously enhancing solid mass arising from the lower pole of the right kidney, distorting the renal contour — appearances of renal cell carcinoma.
🎓 Exam pearl. Visible haematuria over 45 = CT urogram (upper tract) PLUS flexible cystoscopy (bladder) on a 2-week-wait. The excretory phase is the money shot — a filling defect in the opacified collecting system is a urothelial (TCC) tumour, an enhancing renal mass is RCC. Never blame frank haematuria on a UTI in the at-risk adult without imaging.
Suspected renal (ureteric) colic is one of the most common acute urology presentations. NICE recommends an urgent low-dose non-contrast CT KUB (kidneys, ureters, bladder) as the first-line, gold-standard investigation, ideally within 24 hours of presentation. Almost every calculus is visible on CT — including radiolucent uric acid stones that are invisible on plain film — with only rare indinavir stones being CT-occult.
1Recognise the presentation
Classic history is sudden, severe, colicky loin-to-groin pain in a patient who is restless and writhing (unlike peritonitis, where they lie still), often with nausea, vomiting and haematuria (frank or dipstick). Stones lodge at the three anatomical narrowings of the ureter.
🔺PUJ
Pelvi-ureteric junction — where renal pelvis meets ureter.
🔺Pelvic brim
Where the ureter crosses the iliac vessels / pelvic brim.
🔺VUJ
Vesico-ureteric junction — the narrowest point and commonest site of impaction.
2Read the CT KUB systematically
Look for the dense calcific focus within the ureter, then hunt for the secondary signs of obstruction that confirm it is clinically significant.
HydronephrosisHydroureterPerinephric fat strandingSoft-tissue rim sign
Dense focus + hydronephrosis + fat stranding→obstructing ureteric calculus
The "soft-tissue rim sign" (ureteric wall oedema around the stone) helps distinguish a true ureteric stone from a pelvic phlebolith.
3Let size and position guide management
Report the stone size and position — both predict spontaneous passage and steer treatment.
  • <5 mm — usually pass spontaneously; conservative management.
  • 5–10 mm — may pass; medical expulsive therapy with an alpha-blocker (e.g. tamsulosin) for distal stones.
  • >10 mm — unlikely to pass; needs intervention.
4Treat the pain, then the stone
First-line analgesia is an NSAID (e.g. PR diclofenac), with antiemetics and fluids. Definitive stone treatment escalates by size: ESWL (shockwave lithotripsy), ureteroscopy, or PCNL (percutaneous nephrolithotomy) for large or staghorn stones.
💊Conservative
NSAID + fluids ± tamsulosin for small distal stones.
⚡ESWL / URS
Shockwave or ureteroscopy for intermediate stones.
🏥PCNL
For large / staghorn calculi.
🚩
An obstructed, infected kidney (obstructing stone + fever/sepsis or pyonephrosis) is a urological emergency — give IV antibiotics and arrange urgent decompression (nephrostomy or ureteric stent). Bilateral obstruction, or obstruction of a single or transplant kidney, causes acute kidney injury and also needs urgent decompression. In an older patient, never miss a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) masquerading as "renal colic".

🎓 Exam pearl. Low-dose non-contrast CT KUB is first-line and gold-standard for suspected renal colic — it detects nearly all stones, including radiolucent uric acid stones invisible on X-ray. Confirm significance with secondary obstruction signs (hydronephrosis, hydroureter, fat stranding). The two must-not-miss traps are the infected obstructed kidney (emergency decompression) and a leaking AAA mimicking colic in the older patient.
CT__GI & Vascular:
A CT mesenteric angiogram is an arterial-phase CT (often with additional venous/delayed phases) that opacifies the coeliac axis, superior mesenteric artery (SMA), inferior mesenteric artery (IMA) and the mesenteric/portal veins. Its three finals-relevant uses are acute mesenteric ischaemia, acute GI bleeding (active extravasation), and chronic mesenteric ischaemia ("intestinal angina").
1Acute mesenteric ischaemia — the key indication
Suspect in sudden severe abdominal pain out of proportion to examination with a raised lactate and metabolic acidosis, especially with AF or vascular disease. CT angiography shows the arterial filling defect / occlusion and, later, signs of established bowel ischaemia.
🫀SMA embolus
Commonest cause; often cardiac source (AF). Sudden onset.
🧱SMA thrombosis
On atherosclerosis; may have prior intestinal angina.
🩸Venous thrombosis
Mesenteric vein clot in prothrombotic states; subacute.
📉Non-occlusive
Low-flow / shock; patent vessels but poor perfusion.
2Late signs of established bowel necrosis
Once ischaemia is advanced, look for:
  • Bowel-wall non-enhancement (loss of mucosal enhancement)
  • Pneumatosis intestinalis (gas within the bowel wall)
  • Portal venous gas — an ominous late sign
Pneumatosis + portal venous gas→transmural infarction; surgical emergency
3Acute GI bleeding — localising the blush
In a haemodynamically significant lower GI or obscure bleed, CT angiography can localise active contrast extravasation into the bowel lumen — a "blush". This requires a brisk bleeding rate to be positive and guides catheter angiography / embolisation or surgery.
Luminal contrast blushGuides embolisationNeeds active bleed
4Management once diagnosed
Ischaemia: resuscitation, revascularisation (embolectomy / endovascular) and resection of necrotic bowel. GI bleed: resuscitate, then transcatheter embolisation of the culprit vessel or surgery. Both carry high mortality if intervention is delayed.
🚩
Acute mesenteric ischaemia is a time-critical surgical emergency: pain out of proportion + AF/vascular risk + raised lactate mandates urgent CT angiography, resuscitation and vascular/surgical intervention. A massive GI bleed with instability needs resuscitation and urgent CT angiography → embolisation/surgery.

📷 Image placeholder — axial arterial-phase CT of a lower GI bleed showing a focal contrast "blush" (active extravasation) pooling within the sigmoid colon lumen.
🎓 Exam pearl. "Pain out of proportion to examination" + AF + raised lactate = acute mesenteric ischaemia until proven otherwise — the investigation of choice is CT mesenteric angiography, and SMA embolus is the commonest cause. In GI bleeding, a positive scan needs active, brisk bleeding to show the blush.
CT colonography (CTC), also called "virtual colonoscopy", is a CT study of the colon performed after bowel preparation and colonic insufflation (gas/CO2 via a rectal catheter to distend the bowel), reconstructed as 2D images and a 3D "fly-through". It is the main radiological alternative to colonoscopy for detecting colorectal cancer and polyps, particularly in the frail or after an incomplete colonoscopy.
1How it is done
The patient takes bowel preparation (often with oral contrast faecal tagging) so residual stool can be distinguished from true lesions. The colon is then insufflated with CO2 through a soft rectal catheter to distend it, and CT is acquired supine and prone to move mobile stool and fluid. A radiologist reviews both 2D slices and a 3D endoluminal fly-through. IV contrast is added when staging a known/suspected cancer.
Distension and dual positioning are what make small polyps visible.
2When to choose CTC over colonoscopy
CTC is preferred when colonoscopy is unsuitable or incomplete:
🧓Frail / elderly
Better tolerated; no sedation needed.
⛔Incomplete scope
Obstructing tumour or tortuous colon blocking the scope.
🔎Proximal colon
Assess bowel beyond an obstructing distal cancer.
Also for patients who decline or cannot tolerate colonoscopy.
3What it shows
Colorectal carcinoma classically appears as an "apple-core" annular constricting lesion or a polypoid mass; polyps appear as filling defects or protrusions from the wall. CTC also demonstrates diverticular disease and, with IV contrast, allows staging (local extent, nodes, liver/lung metastases).
Annular narrowing + shouldered edges→"apple-core" = colorectal cancer until proven otherwise
Apple-core lesionPolypoid massFilling defect
4Key limitation vs colonoscopy
CTC is diagnostic only — it cannot take a biopsy or perform polypectomy. Any suspicious lesion still needs colonoscopy for tissue diagnosis and removal.
  • UK bowel-cancer screening: FIT (faecal immunochemical test) → colonoscopy, with CTC where colonoscopy is unsuitable.
  • Red-flag symptoms (change in bowel habit, rectal bleeding, weight loss, iron-deficiency anaemia, abdominal/rectal mass) → 2-week-wait referral.
🚩
A suspicious colorectal mass on CTC is cancer until proven otherwise — it needs tissue diagnosis (colonoscopy/biopsy), staging and referral to the colorectal MDT. A complete or impending large-bowel obstruction from an annular tumour is a surgical emergency. CTC is relatively contraindicated in acute severe colitis or when perforation risk is high, because insufflation can perforate the inflamed/weakened bowel.

📷 Image placeholder — 2D coronal CTC image of the sigmoid colon showing a short, annular constricting "apple-core" lesion with shouldered margins and luminal narrowing, typical of colorectal carcinoma.
🎓 Exam pearl. CTC = bowel prep + CO2 insufflation, the go-to alternative to colonoscopy for colorectal cancer/polyps in the frail or after an incomplete scope. Learn the "apple-core" sign, and remember CTC cannot biopsy — a suspicious lesion always returns to colonoscopy for tissue, then MDT.
CT enterography (CTE) is a dedicated small-bowel CT protocol. The patient drinks a large volume of neutral oral contrast (water or a mannitol-type agent) to distend the small bowel, and receives IV contrast, so that mural (bowel-wall) enhancement and thickening stand out against the low-density lumen. Its main role is Crohn's disease — mapping extent, activity and complications — plus small-bowel tumours and obscure GI bleeding.
1Why the neutral oral contrast?
Unlike positive (dense) oral contrast, a neutral agent stays low-density in the lumen. This lets you see mucosal hyperenhancement and mural thickening without the bright lumen masking wall detail. Adequate luminal distension is essential — a collapsed loop can mimic or hide disease.
Neutral oral contrast+ IV contrastDistended small bowel
2Signs of active Crohn's
Active inflammation shows as mural thickening with mucosal hyperenhancement, the comb sign (engorged vasa recta / mesenteric hypervascularity), and fibrofatty proliferation ("creeping fat"). Disease is typically discontinuous with skip lesions and terminal-ileal involvement.
🔥Mural hyperenhancement
Bright, thickened wall = active inflammation
🪮Comb sign
Engorged vasa recta combing the mesentery
🥓Creeping fat
Fibrofatty proliferation around affected loops
3Complications & active vs fibrotic
CTE detects strictures (with pre-stenotic dilatation), fistulae, sinus tracts and abscesses. Crucially it helps separate active inflammatory disease (enhancing, oedematous wall — treat medically) from fibrotic stricturing (non-enhancing, fixed narrowing — often needs surgery/dilatation).
Enhancing, oedematous wall→Active — escalate medical therapy
Fixed narrowing, no enhancement→Fibrotic — surgical / endoscopic management
4CTE vs MRI enterography
CT enterography is quick and widely available — useful acutely or when the patient is unwell. MRI enterography is preferred in younger patients and for repeated follow-up as it avoids ionising radiation. Diagnosis is confirmed by endoscopy and biopsy; faecal calprotectin is used to monitor activity between scans.
  • Prefer MRI enterography for young patients needing repeat imaging
  • CTE better tolerated / faster in the acute setting
Remember Crohn's is transmural, mouth-to-anus (esp. terminal ileum), with skip lesions and non-caseating granulomas.
🚩
Flag complications of Crohn's: a stricture causing bowel obstruction, an intra-abdominal abscess, or a fistula — these may need urgent drainage or surgery and MDT input. A severe active flare needs escalation of therapy. Always consider radiation dose and favour MRI enterography for young patients requiring repeated imaging.

🎓 Exam pearl. CT enterography = neutral oral contrast to distend the small bowel + IV contrast, chiefly for Crohn's. Look for mural thickening with hyperenhancement, the comb sign, creeping fat, strictures, fistulae and abscesses. It distinguishes active (medical) from fibrotic (surgical) disease. Choose MRI enterography for young patients needing repeat imaging to spare radiation.
The adrenal washout CT is a dedicated protocol to characterise an adrenal incidentaloma — an adrenal lesion found unexpectedly on imaging (common, and usually benign). It acquires non-contrast, portal-venous (~60–75s) and delayed (~15 min) images to measure how quickly a lesion washes out contrast, separating a benign adenoma from a sinister non-adenoma (metastasis, phaeochromocytoma, adrenocortical carcinoma). Two questions run in parallel: is it malignant? and is it hormonally active?
1Start with non-contrast attenuation (HU)
Measure the Hounsfield units on the non-contrast phase. A lesion with low attenuation ≤10 HU is a lipid-rich adenoma — benign, and no further characterisation is needed. Fat-rich tissue is dark; adenomas are packed with intracytoplasmic lipid. If attenuation is >10 HU (lipid-poor), you cannot stop here — proceed to washout.
Non-contrast ≤10 HU→Lipid-rich adenoma, stop
2Calculate washout for lipid-poor lesions
Adenomas enhance and de-enhance (wash out) rapidly; non-adenomas hold contrast. Using the three phases, calculate absolute washout ([venous − delayed] / [venous − non-contrast]) or relative washout ([venous − delayed] / venous). A high absolute washout ≥60% or relative washout ≥40% indicates a benign adenoma. Low/poor washout points to a non-adenoma — metastasis, phaeochromocytoma or adrenocortical carcinoma.
Absolute washout ≥60%Relative washout ≥40%
3Read the morphology — size and character
Even with reassuring density, weigh the size and morphology. Features of concern raise the risk of adrenocortical carcinoma or metastasis (adrenals are a common metastatic site — lung, breast). Serial imaging showing rapid growth is a strong warning sign.
🔺Large size >4 cm
Rising malignancy risk; strongly favours carcinoma.
🔺Irregular & heterogeneous
Necrosis, calcification or ill-defined margins.
🔺Rapid growth
Interval enlargement on serial scans is sinister.
4Do the functional (hormonal) screen — always
Every incidentaloma needs a biochemical work-up for hormone excess, regardless of how benign it looks on CT:
  • Phaeochromocytoma — plasma or 24h urinary metanephrines.
  • Cushing's syndrome — overnight dexamethasone suppression test.
  • Conn's / primary hyperaldosteronism — aldosterone:renin ratio, especially with hypertension or hypokalaemia.
A functioning tumour may need surgery even when imaging is benign.
🚩
Never biopsy an adrenal mass until phaeochromocytoma is excluded biochemically. Needle biopsy or manipulation of an unblocked phaeo can precipitate a life-threatening hypertensive crisis. A large (>4 cm), irregular or rapidly growing adrenal mass is worrying for adrenocortical carcinoma or metastasis and needs urgent endocrine/MDT referral — always complete the functional screen first.

(non-contrast HU ≤10 = adenoma; otherwise absolute washout ≥60% or relative ≥40% = adenoma; low washout, >4 cm, irregular or growing = worry) and functional? (metanephrines, overnight dexamethasone suppression, aldosterone:renin ratio). The single most-tested safety point: exclude phaeo before any biopsy or surgery.
CT__MSK / Limbs:
CT of the upper limb gives high-resolution bony detail with multiplanar and 3D reconstructions. It is used to characterise complex and intra-articular fractures and for pre-operative planning where plain films are insufficient — showing the number and position of fragments, articular step, comminution and displacement that a 2D X-ray cannot fully resolve.
1Occult scaphoid fracture
The scaphoid is a key cause of an occult wrist fracture. A patient with anatomical snuffbox tenderness but a normal initial X-ray is treated as a clinical scaphoid fracture: immobilise and re-image with CT or MRI to detect the fracture. The scaphoid has a retrograde blood supply, so proximal pole fractures risk avascular necrosis (AVN) and non-union.
Snuffbox tenderness + normal X-ray→Immobilise & re-image (CT/MRI)
2Complex distal radius fractures
CT characterises intra-articular extension, comminution and displacement of distal radius fractures. It quantifies the articular step and fragment position to guide operative fixation (e.g. volar plating) where plain films underestimate joint involvement.
Intra-articular stepComminutionFragment position
3Elbow, scapula & glenoid
CT clarifies radial head fractures, complex intra-articular distal humerus fractures and the terrible triad (radial head fracture + coronoid fracture + elbow dislocation). It is also the modality of choice for scapula/glenoid fractures, where overlapping bony anatomy obscures the plain film.
  • Radial head and comminuted distal humerus
  • Terrible triad of the elbow
  • Glenoid articular involvement
4Union & hardware assessment
CT is superior to plain films for assessing fracture union vs non-union, bridging callus and the position of metalwork. It confirms adequate reduction and detects hardware complications such as intra-articular screw penetration.
🦴Union check
Bridging callus, persistent lucency = non-union.
🔩Hardware
Screw position, intra-articular penetration.
🚩
A clinically suspected scaphoid fracture with a normal X-ray must NOT be dismissed — immobilise and re-image (CT/MRI) to avoid a missed fracture progressing to non-union or AVN. An open fracture, or any fracture with neurovascular compromise or compartment syndrome, is a surgical emergency requiring urgent orthopaedic input.

🎓 Exam pearl. Snuffbox tenderness + normal X-ray = treat as scaphoid fracture: immobilise and re-image with CT/MRI. Remember the retrograde blood supply — proximal pole fractures are highest risk for AVN and non-union. For all complex/intra-articular upper limb fractures, CT defines articular step, comminution and fragment position in 3D to plan fixation.
CT of the lower limb characterises complex and intra-articular fractures for surgical planning, where plain films consistently underestimate articular depression, comminution and fragment position. It renders the injury in 3D, guiding whether and how to fix the joint surface.
1TIBIAL PLATEAU — quantify the joint
CT measures articular depression and split width that plain films miss, and refines the Schatzker classification to plan fixation.
High-energy plateau fracture→watch for COMPARTMENT SYNDROME
2PILON & ANKLE — the plafond and posterior malleolus
Pilon (distal tibial plafond) fractures follow axial load and are typically comminuted at the articular surface. In trimalleolar ankle injuries, CT sizes the posterior malleolus fragment to decide if it needs fixation.
Articular step-offComminutionFragment position
3CALCANEAL — measure Böhler's angle, check the spine
Classically a fall from height / axial load. On the lateral view and CT, Böhler's angle is reduced or flattened in fracture. These are frequently bilateral and associated with spinal and other axial injuries — always image the lumbar spine.
Calcaneal fracture from a fall→search for associated spinal fracture
4FOOT & FOLLOW-UP — talus, Lisfranc, union & hardware
CT clarifies subtle talus and Lisfranc (tarsometatarsal) injuries and assesses union and hardware position post-operatively.
🦴Tibial plateau
Depression/split; Schatzker; compartment risk.
🦶Calcaneal
Fall from height; flat Böhler's; check spine.
🚩
High-energy lower-limb fractures (especially tibial plateau/shaft) risk acute compartment syndrome: pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch and a tense compartment — a limb-threatening emergency needing urgent fasciotomy. Do NOT wait for pulselessness (a late sign). Open fractures and any neurovascular compromise need urgent orthoplastic input, and a calcaneal fracture from a fall should prompt a search for associated spinal fractures.

CT of the bony pelvis is the gold standard for characterising pelvic ring and acetabular fractures — it is far more sensitive than plain films for the posterior ring (sacrum and SI joints) and provides the classification and 3D detail needed for surgical planning. In the polytrauma patient it doubles as a search for active bleeding and associated visceral injury.
1Pelvic ring: it breaks in TWO places
The pelvis is a ring, so a single disruption is mechanically rare — a break at one point almost always means a second break (or ligamentous disruption) elsewhere. High-energy mechanisms (RTC, fall from height) dominate. CT defines the exact pattern for the Young-Burgess classification, which groups injuries by the direction of force.
↔️Lateral compression (LC)
Side-on force; horizontal pubic rami fractures with sacral impaction. Often reduces pelvic volume.
📖APC / open-book
AP force springs the ring open: pubic symphysis diastasis + SI joint disruption. Massively raised volume → catastrophic haemorrhage.
⬆️Vertical shear (VS)
Axial force displaces a hemipelvis vertically; most unstable, high bleeding risk.
2Acetabular fractures: columns and walls
Acetabular fractures are intra-articular and demand anatomical reduction to prevent post-traumatic arthritis. CT with 3D reconstruction defines involvement of the anterior/posterior column and anterior/posterior wall (the Judet-Letournel scheme), directing the surgical approach and fixation.
Anterior columnPosterior columnAnterior wallPosterior wall
3CT angiography: hunt the bleeder
A CT angiogram of the pelvis in the arterial phase identifies active arterial extravasation — a contrast blush — which flags a patient who may benefit from angio-embolisation rather than open surgery. Note that pelvic haemorrhage is often venous (from the presacral plexus) or from the fracture surfaces themselves, controlled by tamponade from a binder.
Contrast blush on arterial phase→Interventional radiology for embolisation
4Associated injuries: look beyond bone
Pelvic ring disruption carries a high burden of visceral and vascular injury that CT helps detect.
  • Urethral injury — blood at the meatus, high-riding prostate, scrotal/perineal bruising. Do NOT catheterise until excluded → retrograde urethrogram.
  • Bladder rupture (intra- vs extraperitoneal) — CT cystogram.
  • Open injury via rectum or vagina — mandates examination.
  • Major iliac vessels and lumbosacral plexus.
An unstable, haemodynamically compromised patient must not be delayed for CT.
🚩
An unstable pelvic ring fracture with haemodynamic instability is a life-threatening emergency. Apply a pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters (not the iliac crests), resuscitate via the major haemorrhage protocol, and arrange urgent angio-embolisation or surgery. Suspected urethral injury (blood at meatus) contraindicates urethral catheterisation until assessed. Never delay a haemodynamically unstable patient for CT.

A CT peripheral angiogram (“run-off”) images the arterial tree from the aorta through the iliacs and down the legs to the feet using timed IV contrast. It maps stenoses, occlusions and collaterals to localise disease and plan revascularisation — angioplasty/stent versus bypass. Core uses: peripheral arterial disease (PAD), acute limb ischaemia and vascular trauma.
1Map the level of disease in PAD
CT run-off localises the culprit segment so treatment can be targeted. Read it in three tiers: aortoiliac, femoropopliteal and infrapopliteal (crural). Look for stenoses, complete occlusions and the collaterals that reconstitute vessels beyond an occlusion.
AortoiliacFemoropoplitealInfrapopliteal
Short focal stenosis→Endovascular angioplasty/stent
Long occlusion / multilevel disease→Surgical bypass
2The claudication → critical ischaemia spectrum
Chronic limb ischaemia runs from intermittent claudication (calf pain on walking, relieved by rest) to critical limb ischaemia — rest pain (worse at night, relieved by hanging the foot out of bed), ulceration and gangrene. Quantify with the ABPI.
  • ABPI <0.9 = PAD; a very low value signals critical ischaemia.
  • ABPI >1.2 may be falsely elevated by incompressible calcified vessels in diabetes — do not be reassured.
Risk factors: smoking, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia. Best medical therapy (antiplatelet, statin, smoking cessation, supervised exercise) underpins all management.
3Acute limb ischaemia — the 6 Ps
A sudden arterial cut-off, embolic (often AF) or thrombotic (on background PAD). Recognise the 6 Ps: Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Perishingly cold, Paraesthesia and Paralysis. The last two mark a threatened or irreversible limb.
🫐Embolic
Sudden onset, AF or post-MI, no prior claudication, sharp cut-off with clean vessels above.
🩸Thrombotic
On chronic PAD, diffusely diseased vessels and established collaterals; less abrupt.
4Vascular trauma
In penetrating or high-energy blunt injury, CT angiography identifies arterial transection, active contrast extravasation (bleeding), intimal flaps and pseudoaneurysm, and defines whether flow to the limb is preserved — guiding urgent surgical or endovascular repair.
🚩
Acute limb ischaemia is a surgical emergency. The 6 Ps — especially paraesthesia and paralysis — signal a threatened or irreversible limb, with irreversible damage after roughly 6 hours. Give IV heparin, make an urgent vascular referral, and revascularise (embolectomy or thrombolysis) within hours. Likewise critical limb ischaemia (rest pain, ulceration, tissue loss) needs urgent revascularisation to save the limb.

Sudden painful cold pulseless leg in an AF patient = embolic acute limb ischaemia until proven otherwise: heparinise and refer, don’t wait. CT run-off doesn’t just diagnose — it maps the level (aortoiliac vs femoropopliteal vs infrapopliteal) to decide stent versus bypass.
CT__Whole Body / Specialised:
The trauma pan-scan (whole-body CT) is a single, protocolised CT run covering head to pelvis in a major-trauma patient, designed to rapidly detect all life-threatening injuries in one pass. Its core purpose is to convert an unpredictable, multi-region injury pattern into a systematic, prioritised problem list within minutes of arrival.
1INDICATION & THE STABILITY GATEKEEPER
Whole-body CT is indicated in major trauma with a significant mechanism (RTC, fall from height, high-energy blunt/penetrating injury) once the ATLS primary survey has secured the airway, breathing and circulation. The absolute prerequisite is that the patient is haemodynamically stable enough to tolerate the scanner — the CT room is a hostile, resource-poor environment. The scan answers "what is injured and how badly?" but must never delay definitive haemorrhage control.
Stable / transient responder, cleared primary survey→Proceed to pan-scan
Persistent hypotension despite resuscitation→Theatre / IR, NOT the scanner
2THE STANDARD PROTOCOL
A trauma pan-scan is a sequenced acquisition, not one uniform scan. It classically comprises a non-contrast head and cervical spine (contrast obscures blood and is unnecessary for bone/brain injury) followed by contrast-enhanced chest, abdomen and pelvis. Abdominal imaging is often dual-phase — an arterial phase to catch active arterial bleeding and vascular injury, and a portal-venous phase for solid-organ parenchyma and venous bleeding. A delayed phase may be added to distinguish active extravasation from contained pseudoaneurysm and to assess the collecting system/bladder.
Non-contrast head + C-spineArterial phase chest/abdo — vascular injury, blushPortal-venous abdo/pelvis — organs, free fluid

3SYSTEMATIC REVIEW FOR LIFE-THREATENING INJURY
Read the pan-scan region by region with a fixed search pattern so nothing is missed. Prioritise the immediately fatal injuries first.
🧠Intracranial haemorrhage
Extradural, subdural, SAH, contusion; look for midline shift and effaced basal cisterns.
🦴C-spine fracture
Assess alignment on sagittal reformats; any fracture = unstable until proven otherwise.
❤️Aortic injury
Mediastinal haematoma, contour irregularity or pseudoaneurysm at the isthmus.
🫁Haemo/pneumothorax
Occult pneumothoraces are common; tension physiology needs immediate decompression.
🩸Solid-organ injury + blush
Splenic/hepatic/renal laceration; a contrast blush = active extravasation needing IR/surgery.
🦵Pelvic fracture + free fluid
Unstable pelvic ring injury bleeds massively; free fluid without organ injury suggests hollow-viscus or mesenteric injury.
📷 Image placeholder — arterial-phase axial abdominal CT of the spleen showing a parenchymal laceration with a focus of high-density contrast pooling (active extravasation / blush) and surrounding perisplenic free fluid.
4PAN-SCAN vs SELECTIVE IMAGING
The debate weighs speed and completeness against radiation and cost. Pan-scan is fast, catches clinically occult injuries and is favoured in high-energy blunt polytrauma; randomised evidence found no overall mortality benefit over selective scanning, but confirmed it is quicker to a full diagnosis. Selective CT (targeted to clinical/examination findings) reduces radiation dose and is preferred in stable patients with a low-energy mechanism, a reliable examination, or in children/young adults where lifetime radiation risk matters. The decision is individualised to mechanism, physiology and examination reliability.
🚩
Do not delay a haemodynamically unstable patient for CT. The scanner is a dangerous place for a bleeding patient — a persistent non-responder to resuscitation with an obvious source (positive FAST, unstable pelvis, penetrating torso wound) belongs in theatre or interventional radiology for haemorrhage control, not queuing for imaging. "CT is a tunnel of death" for the exsanguinating patient: resuscitate and control bleeding first.
🎓 Exam pearl. The single most-tested principle is patient selection: a stable trauma patient gets a whole-body CT to map every injury, but an unstable one is resuscitated and taken for definitive haemorrhage control first. On the scan itself, an arterial-phase contrast blush in a solid organ signals active bleeding and upgrades management towards embolisation or surgery.
A staging CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis (CT CAP) is the workhorse cross-sectional scan used to map how far a solid cancer has spread. In one contrast-enhanced acquisition it assesses the primary tumour, regional and distant lymph nodes, and the commonest sites of distant metastasis, generating the anatomical data that drives the TNM stage and the MDT treatment decision.
1WHY WE STAGE — TNM AND THE MDT
Staging answers a single question: how extensive is this cancer? The answer is encoded as TNM — T (size and local invasion of the primary tumour), N (regional nodal disease), and M (distant metastasis). CT CAP is chosen because it covers the three body cavities where most solid tumours seed, is fast, widely available and reproducible. The report is the substrate of the multidisciplinary team (MDT) meeting, where surgeons, oncologists, radiologists and pathologists agree on whether disease is curative/resectable or palliative. Stage — not merely histology — determines whether a patient is offered radical surgery, neoadjuvant chemotherapy or best supportive care.
M1 disease found (distant mets)→usually shifts intent from curative to systemic/palliative
2THE PROTOCOL — CONTRAST AND PHASE
A standard staging CT is acquired after intravenous iodinated contrast in the portal-venous phase (~60–70 s post-injection). At this timing the liver parenchyma, spleen, bowel wall and lymph nodes enhance maximally, making hypovascular liver metastases (which stay relatively dark against bright liver) and nodal disease conspicuous. Oral contrast or water may distend bowel; some protocols add an arterial phase for hypervascular tumours (e.g. HCC, neuroendocrine, renal). Adequate renal function and no contrast allergy must be checked before the scan. Images are reviewed on soft-tissue, lung and bone windows so no compartment is missed.

3READING FOR METASTASES — WHERE CANCER GOES
Metastatic disease follows predictable routes; the reporting radiologist systematically checks each. Common patterns:
🫁Lung
Rounded pulmonary nodules, often multiple/basal (haematogenous seeding).
🩸Liver
Hypodense lesions in portal-venous phase; commonest visceral GI met site.
🔺Adrenal
Nodular thickening — classic in lung cancer; distinguish from benign adenoma.
🦴Bone
Lytic or sclerotic deposits in spine/pelvis (review bone windows).
🕸️Peritoneum
Omental caking, nodules, ascites — typical of ovarian/GI spread.
🫘Nodes
Enlarged (>1 cm short axis) or rounded lymph nodes along drainage pathways.
Lymph nodes are judged by short-axis size, shape, clustering and loss of the fatty hilum — size alone is imperfect, which is where PET adds value. Any incidental finding (e.g. an unrelated aneurysm or second lesion) is also flagged.
4RESPONSE, RESTAGING AND CT vs PET vs MRI
Beyond baseline staging, CT CAP is repeated to assess treatment response. Under the RECIST framework, a small number of target lesions are measured (longest diameter) at baseline and re-measured on follow-up scans; the summed change classifies disease as complete/partial response, stable disease or progression. This standardises decisions and trial reporting. Restaging before surgery or at relapse uses the same protocol. Know the modality niches:
CT the anatomical workhorse — fast, whole-body coverage, structural detail.PET-CT adds metabolic (18F-FDG) activity — better for occult nodal/distant disease, characterising indeterminate lesions, and lymphoma/lung staging.MRI superior soft-tissue contrast — local staging of rectal, prostate, liver and brain disease.

🚩
A staging CT can reveal an impending oncological emergency that needs action before staging is even finalised. Look for malignant SVC obstruction (mediastinal mass compressing the SVC with collateral veins — facial swelling, distended neck veins), spinal cord / cauda equina compression from vertebral or epidural deposits (needs urgent MRI, steroids and referral), and a large pericardial effusion (risk of tamponade) or massive pleural effusion. These are time-critical — communicate them urgently rather than filing them in the routine report.
🎓 Exam pearl. CT CAP in the portal-venous phase is the anatomical workhorse for solid-tumour staging: it maps TNM, drives the MDT, and tracks response via RECIST target lesions. Reach for PET-CT when you need metabolic characterisation of nodes or occult mets, and MRI for local soft-tissue staging (rectum, prostate, liver, brain) — and never let an SVC obstruction, cord compression or effusion slip past unactioned.
18F-FDG PET-CT is a hybrid functional-anatomical scan that maps glucose metabolism across the whole body: a radiolabelled glucose analogue lights up metabolically active tissue, while a co-registered CT pins each hot spot to an anatomical location. Its dominant role is cancer staging, restaging and treatment-response assessment.
1HOW IT WORKS — TRAPPED GLUCOSE LIGHTS UP
18F-FDG (fluorodeoxyglucose) is a glucose analogue tagged with the positron-emitter fluorine-18. It is taken up by glucose-avid cells via GLUT transporters and phosphorylated by hexokinase to FDG-6-phosphate — but, unlike glucose, it cannot proceed down glycolysis and is metabolically trapped inside the cell. Highly metabolic tissues (many cancers, sites of infection and inflammation) therefore accumulate tracer and appear as focal hot spots. The PET component detects the annihilation photons from positron decay to build a functional map; the CT supplies the anatomy and attenuation correction, and the two are fused so function and structure are read together.
SUV (standardised uptake value) a semi-quantitative index of uptake normalised to injected dose and body weight; SUVmax lets you compare lesions and track response, though it is affected by blood glucose, uptake time and technique.
glucose-avid tumour→FDG trapped → focal high-SUV hot spot on fused image

2WHAT IT IS USED FOR
The workhorse of PET-CT is oncology. Key indications:
🎯Staging / restaging
Whole-body assessment of nodal and distant metastatic spread, e.g. lung cancer, lymphoma, oesophageal and head & neck cancers.
🔍Characterising lesions
Helping tell benign from malignant in an indeterminate lung nodule or adrenal mass by degree of avidity.
📈Response assessment
Comparing pre- and post-treatment uptake — falling SUV / loss of avidity suggests response (e.g. interim PET in Hodgkin lymphoma).
❓Unknown primary
Hunting the occult primary in cancer of unknown primary presenting with metastases.
Beyond cancer, FDG PET-CT is used in infection and inflammation: localising the source in pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO), mapping large-vessel vasculitis (e.g. giant cell arteritis / Takayasu), and assessing suspected prosthetic-graft or device infection.
PUO, negative first-line work-up→FDG PET-CT to localise occult infection, inflammation or malignancy
3PITFALLS — FALSE POSITIVES & FALSE NEGATIVES
FDG is not tumour-specific — it marks glucose metabolism, so interpretation must account for normal and misleading uptake.
Physiological uptake normal avidity in brain (obligate glucose user), myocardium, brown fat, bowel, and urinary tract (renal excretion into ureters/bladder) can mimic or mask disease.
False positives infection, inflammation, recent surgery, granulomatous disease (e.g. sarcoidosis, TB) and active brown fat all light up despite no cancer.
False negatives low-grade / indolent tumours, mucinous adenocarcinomas, and lesions <~1 cm (below scanner resolution) may be non-avid and missed.
📷 Image placeholder — maximum-intensity-projection (MIP) whole-body PET showing expected physiological uptake: bright brain and myocardium, tracer in kidneys, ureters and bladder, plus symmetrical supraclavicular brown-fat activity, contrasted with a discrete pathological nodal focus.
Patient preparation is critical: patients fast for ~6 hours and blood glucose is controlled, because hyperglycaemia competes with FDG and reduces tumour uptake (risking false negatives). Patients rest quietly and are kept warm to limit muscle and brown-fat uptake.
4PRACTICALITIES & SAFETY
PET-CT delivers a meaningful radiation dose (from both the radiotracer and the CT component), so it is justified against clinical benefit. After injection the patient is transiently radioactive: they should avoid close/prolonged contact with pregnant women and young infants for a short period (typically the rest of the day) and follow local advice on hydration to clear tracer via urine. Diabetic patients need careful scheduling and glucose management (timing of insulin/oral agents relative to fasting) to keep blood glucose in range without hypoglycaemia. Pregnancy is a relative contraindication and breastfeeding may need temporary interruption per local protocol.
🚩
A positive PET finding is not a diagnosis. Because FDG avidity is non-specific — infection, inflammation, sarcoid and post-operative change all cause false positives, while low-grade, mucinous and sub-centimetre tumours cause false negatives — an FDG-avid lesion usually requires histological (biopsy) confirmation before it changes management. Do not upstage, deny curative treatment, or diagnose relapse on PET appearances alone.
🎓 Exam pearl. FDG is a glucose analogue that is trapped after phosphorylation, so PET-CT shows metabolism, not malignancy per se. Control the blood glucose (hyperglycaemia → false negatives), remember physiological brain/myocardium/bowel/urinary uptake, and confirm suspicious hot spots with biopsy before acting.
CT-guided percutaneous biopsy uses cross-sectional imaging to advance a needle precisely into a deep lesion and obtain tissue for histological diagnosis when a safe percutaneous window exists. The same principle underlies CT-guided drainage of collections and abscesses. CT gives excellent spatial resolution and lets the operator plan a path that avoids vessels, bowel and pleura.
1INDICATIONS & WHAT IS SAMPLED
CT-guided biopsy obtains tissue from deep or inaccessible targets: lung nodules/masses, liver lesions, bone, and retroperitoneal or nodal masses. The choice is between core-needle biopsy (a spring-loaded cutting needle giving a tissue core that preserves architecture — needed for lymphoma subtyping, tumour grading and immunohistochemistry) and fine-needle aspiration (FNA) (a thin needle giving cells for cytology, quicker but less tissue). CT is also used to place a Seldinger drain into an abscess or collection for both diagnosis and treatment.
Need architecture / IHC (?lymphoma)→core-needle biopsy, not FNA
🎯Core biopsy
Tissue core, preserves histology, higher diagnostic yield
💧FNA
Cells for cytology, quick, lower morbidity
🚿Drain
Seldinger catheter into abscess/collection

2PRE-PROCEDURE CHECKS
Confirm the indication and that biopsy was an MDT decision that will change management, and that the target is still the best/safest lesion on current imaging. Obtain informed consent, documenting the specific risks (bleeding, pneumothorax, infection, seeding, pain). Crucially, check coagulation status: platelets and INR/clotting, and stop antiplatelets and anticoagulants in advance per local protocol (e.g. hold clopidogrel/DOACs, bridge or reverse warfarin, correct thrombocytopenia).
PlateletsINRMeds review
INR raised / on DOAC or clopidogrel→correct or withhold before biopsy — never proceed blind
3TECHNIQUE
Position the patient for the shortest safe route and infiltrate local anaesthetic to skin and deeper tissues. The operator plans the needle path to avoid vessels, bowel and pleura, minimising the number of times pleura is crossed in lung biopsy. The needle is advanced in stages, with repeated CT to confirm the needle tip is within the target before firing the core device or aspirating. For drainage, a guidewire is passed (Seldinger technique) and the catheter railroaded into the collection and secured.
📷 Image placeholder — CT confirmation image showing the biopsy needle tip lying centrally within a hepatic segment VII lesion, with the trajectory avoiding intervening major hepatic vessels.
4COMPLICATIONS & POST-PROCEDURE CARE
Counsel for and monitor: bleeding/haemorrhage (esp. vascular liver/renal lesions), pneumothorax (the most common significant complication of lung biopsy), infection, pain, and the rare risk of tumour seeding along the needle track. Observe the patient afterwards; following lung biopsy perform an erect chest X-ray (typically ~1 hour later) to exclude a delayed pneumothorax before discharge.
🚩
Pneumothorax after lung biopsy — new breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain or hypoxia signals a pneumothorax that may require a chest drain. Also watch for uncontrolled bleeding (tachycardia, hypotension, falling Hb). And never biopsy without checking coagulation — uncorrected clotting derangement is a leading cause of catastrophic haemorrhage.
🎓 Exam pearl. Pneumothorax is the commonest significant complication of CT-guided lung biopsy, so an erect CXR post-procedure is mandatory; and for any percutaneous biopsy always confirm platelets and INR and stop antiplatelets/anticoagulants beforehand.
